To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the feasibility of measuring triplet phases has been established, that the number of triplet phases that can be measured in a typical experiment is limited by the available crystal volume rather than by the number of reflections that can be collected, and that the number of triplets that can be measured from a crystal of a small protein is sufficient for structure solution.
a total of 850 triplet phases can be measured from a small protein and that about 750 single phase values can be derived from these triplet phases.
the feasibility of measuring a large enough set of triplet phases to solve the structure has been demonstrated, and that the measured phases are of sufficient accuracy to solve the structure.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the measurement of a set of triplet phase angles large enough to solve a small protein structure.
the feasibility of measuring a large set of triplets from small protein crystals and with the feasibility of using this information to solve their structure.
the feasibility of measuring a large set of phases from small protein crystals.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the feasibility of measuring a large set of triplets phases from a small crystal of protein has been demonstrated.
the measurement of triplet phases for small protein crystals is feasible and should be pursued.
, at the moment, a large set of triplets cannot be measured for the solution of small protein structure.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the feasibility of solving the structure of a protein from its measured triplet phases has been demonstrated, although the method has not yet been applied to a real protein.
, in spite of the difficulties, the measurement of a set of about 850 triplets from a small protein is possible, and the results are of good quality.
a total of about 1500 triplet phases have been collected from small protein crystals.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is feasible to measure enough triplets to solve the structure from a small protein, but it will require a significant amount of time.
the number of triplet phase measurements required to solve the structure can be reduced to a small fraction of the number of single phases required.
it is possible to measure enough triplet phases to solve the structure from a single protein crystal, provided the crystal diffracts to at least about 2 angstroms.
